subject: Is it usefull to save groups factor scores when equal factor loadings is not supported

messages.author: 9297ddd34865d3bd
messages.subject: Is it usefull to save groups factor scores when equal factor loadings is not supported
parts:
Hi!

First of all, thank you all for your answers to questions that have already been asked in the past.

I conducted a CFA to test the structure of a psychological scale, with group = "level of education". The weak invariance or equal factor loadings is not supported (χ2 = 210 (125) vs χ2 = 285 (157), p < .0001).

Consequently, can I still compute the average of my indicators to create my psychological measure? Or would it be better to extract the factor scores, following the procedure Terrence has described there, to account for that unequal factor loading depending on the level of education?

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: Is it usefull to save groups factor scores when equal factor loadings is not supported
parts:
Do you really need scores for your study? Why don't you search for partial invariance and do your analysis without scores?

Best

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Is it usefull to save groups factor scores when equal factor loadings is not supported
parts:
Measurement invariance tells you about plausibly valid inferences that you can draw from your analysis. Achieving equal loadings would have made it possible to infer that differences in slope parameters are not due to differences in how the groups response to the instrument is related to the underlying latent variable. If you don't establish at least partial invariance, then this remains a plausible alternative explanation for any differences that you observe.
     That really does not have anything to do with factor scores. If you cannot establish at least partial invariance, thenwhatever you do, this will remain a plausible alternative explanation.

messages.author: 9297ddd34865d3bd
messages.subject: Re: Is it usefull to save groups factor scores when equal factor loadings is not supported
parts:
Thanks for all your answers.

After checking the litterature, I finally conclude that I cannot trust the χ2 to compare all 3 models because my sample countains 1,105 respondents. 

With this in mind, overall: 
  • Weak invariance or equal factor loadings seem in fact supported (χ2 = 210 (125) vs χ2 = 285 (157), p < .01; RMSEA difference is .005; CFI difference is -.015; TLI difference is -.008). CFI difference seems large enough to reject the loadings equality, but RMSEA, TLI and even SRMR (which I do not report) show the opposite;
  • Strong invariance or equal intercepts seem strongly also supported (χ2 = 285 (156) vs χ2 = 316 (181), p < .01; RMSEA difference is -.003; CFI difference is -.002; TLI difference is .005);

I understand that:
  1. They are no differences in slope parameters with the level of education;
  2. I can compute the average of my items and go on with my analysis by using the mean of my scale. I do not have to establish (at least) partial invariance, since there is equal loadings and intercepts;

Thanks for your help!

messages.author: ff3a366aa7a9b488
messages.subject: Re: Is it usefull to save groups factor scores when equal factor loadings is not supported
parts:
Terrence has written a couple of nice statements on this in a slightly different context:

"Unfortunately, approximate fit indices (AFIs) or their differences (Δ) between competing models rarely have known sampling distributions. Even when they do [e.g., the root mean-squared error of approximation (RMSEA); Steiger and Lind, 1980], it is often unclear how to interpret the magnitude of a (Δ)AFI. Researchers frequently rely on rule-of-thumb cutoffs, such as those proposed by Hu and Bentler (1999) for AFIs or by Cheung and Rensvold (2002) for ΔAFIs, either based on intuition or derived from simulation studies under specific conditions that might not generalize to the wide array of SEMs encountered in practice. Although it is reasonable to argue that models with only negligible misspecifications should not be rejected, it is unreasonable to expect a single rule-of-thumb cutoff for any (Δ)AFI to perform consistently across various models (Cheung and Lau, 2012; Pornprasertmanit et al., 2013)" (
https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01455/full).


Other sources are easily identifiable. You could ask whether the decrease or increase (godness or badness of fit depending on the AFI) is significant at a chosen level instead of using fixed cut-offs.

Perhaps it would be useful to consult SEMnet, since the issue is somewhat detached from lavaan?


HTH

Christian
